Lessons.Title: Connecting Equations to Graphs (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: connect the coefficients of ax+by=c to line intercepts and rate of change, graph the line and interpret its feasible points in context. Original first-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 10, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/10/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Building On 8.EE.B.6 and HSA-SSE.A.1.a; Addressing HSA-CED.A.3, HSA-CED.A.4, HSA-REI.D.10.

Independent carnival scenario: games cost $2 each and rides cost $5 each. With a $30 spending budget, x games and y rides that use all money satisfy 2x+5y=30. Both counts must be nonnegative integers. The mathematical line has intercepts (15,0) and (0,6); slope -2/5 when solving y=6−(2/5)x. The slope means one additional game requires 0.4 fewer rides on the continuous spending boundary; actual feasible rides are whole counts.

Graph using two intercepts and a labelled shared axis, then list integer feasible combinations: (0,6),(5,4),(10,2),(15,0). The point (3,5) gives 2(3)+5(5)=31 and exceeds the budget; (−5,8) solves the equation algebraically but violates the nonnegative count domain.

Student activity: build original graphs of 2x+5y=30 and x+4y=20 with consistent scales; interpret each intercept and negative slope; defend which points meet real-world restrictions and why points off the line do not spend exactly the budget. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 maximum): correct intercepts, correctly labelled graph, domain/rate interpretation, and valid solution classification with an explicit reason. The physical graph and reasoning are teacher reviewed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Standard form and intercept
KeyConcepts.Definition: For ax+by=c, set one variable to zero to get the other intercept.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Divide only if the associated coefficient is nonzero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Slope from standard form
KeyConcepts.Definition: Solving y=(c−ax)/b produces slope -a/b when b≠0.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain units as change in y per unit x.
KeyConcepts.Example: Here slope is -2/5 rides per game on a continuous line.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discrete feasible values
KeyConcepts.Definition: Whole-number context gives discrete points rather than every continuous location.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check both equation and nonnegative-integer domain.
KeyConcepts.Example: (5,4) is valid; (−5,8) is not a physical choice.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find graph intercepts
WorkedExamples.Question: Find intercepts of 2x+5y=30.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: The line joining them has equation y=6−(2/5)x.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check integer feasible plans
WorkedExamples.Question: Which nonnegative integer choices spend exactly $30?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: Let y=6−(2/5)x, with x between 0 and 15.
Other whole y=1,3,5 give half-integer x and cannot meet exact cost with whole games.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every listed pair satisfies cost equation and domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify wrong and forbidden points
WorkedExamples.Question: Test (3,5) and (−5,8) for the carnival model.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: Thus (3,5) is not on the spending-equality line.
For (−5,8), cost -10+40=30, so it is on the full mathematical line.
But negative five games is impossible, so it is not a valid plan.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Neither is context-feasible: one overspends, one violates domain.
WorkedExamples.Check: Mathematical equation truth is distinct from real-world feasibility.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating slope -2/5 as allowed fractional rides
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The line is continuous, but ride counts are discrete.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing budget equality with at-most budget
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Points below the full-cost line may be affordable without using all funds.

SummaryPoints: Intercepts reveal solutions with one quantity zero.
A context can restrict a continuous line to discrete first-quadrant points.
A graph's scale, domain and costs need teacher-reviewed interpretation.
